extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of 19th-century humorous essays; writers and critics interested in conversational wit and style
extracted.subtask_description: Observational, prescriptive remarks about good conversation, wit, and light humorous essaying drawn from Oliver Wendell Holmes's The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table. Covers attitudes toward puns, repetition, logic, conceit, poetic clichés, and social conversational norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Societies of Mutual Admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: All generous companies of artists, authors, philanthropists, men of science, are, or ought to be, Societies of Mutual Admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such societies unite talented people, promote literature and art, and are a crown of a literary metropolis; examples invoked include Shakespeare/Ben Jonson, Addison and Steele, and Johnson's circle. Exclusivity is not a vice; mutual admiration fosters production and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading conversation with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: All generous minds have a horror of what are commonly called 'facts.' They are the brute beasts of the intellectual domain. 'I allow no "facts" at this table.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts can choke pleasant generalization and abstract thought; conversation should favor broader, generalized ideas rather than tedious literal details (the speaker notes the remark must be 'seasoned' for vulgar minds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequenced, coherent thought over 'jerky' wit
rubrics_metrics.description: There are men of esprit who are excessively exhausting... They say bright things on all possible subjects, but their zigzags rack you to death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid disjointed, rapid associative leaps that fatigue listeners; orderly progression of ideas is less exhausting and preferable. A 'dull but kindly' conversational partner can be a welcome relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of ideas is permissible and often valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: A thought is often original, though you have uttered it a hundred times. The truths a man carries about with him are his tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing an idea is acceptable because new contexts or associative routes can render it fresh; authors need not avoid repeating types or 'stereotypes' of thought when the use is apt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns are socially injurious — generally to be avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: A pun is primâ facie an insult to the person you are talking with. It implies utter indifference to or sublime contempt for his remarks... 'I shall henceforth consider any interruption by a pun as a hint to change my boarding-house.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns derail serious conversation, show disrespect, and are likened to wanton boys placing coins on railroad tracks; Holmes gives a comic legal anecdote (pun leading to a fatal scuffle, trial, and burning of the pun) to emphasize social sanction. Use puns sparingly, if at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic alone is inadequate; prize broad imaginative insight
rubrics_metrics.description: If a logical mind ever found out anything with its logic? ... You can hire logic, in the shape of a lawyer, to prove anything that you want to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical subtlety and rhetorical skill can argue anything but do not substitute for genuine understanding; value minds that couple distant truths and have wide 'span' rather than merely technical logical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate conceit is natural and socially useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk about conceit as much as you like, it is to human character what salt is to the ocean; it keeps it sweet, and renders it endurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certain amount of self-regard makes people cheerful and tolerable; loss of all illusions leaves a person dull and dispirited. The author defends modest conceit as a normal and benign human trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major faults of conversation: lack of ideas/words/manners and long quarrels on fundamental differences
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the great faults of conversation? Want of ideas, want of words, want of manners... I will tell you what I have found spoil more good talks than anything else;—long arguments on special points between people who differ on the fundamental principles upon which these points depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To keep conversation profitable avoid long disputes that arise from clashing ultimate beliefs; establish a 'code of finalities' to prevent arguments about remainders and petty secondary disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware poetic and rhetorical clichés ('album verses')
rubrics_metrics.description: One gets tired to death of the old, old rhymes... Nine tenths of the 'Juvenile Poems' written spring out of the above musical and suggestive coincidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holmes mocks formulaic verse (repeated rhymes like 'day/ay', 'beauty/duty') and warns writers against relying on the same shopworn patterns; the final couplet is often the hardest part ('C’est le dernier pas qui coute').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational exertion has a real physiological cost
rubrics_metrics.description: This business of conversation is a very serious matter... It is better to lose a pint of blood from your veins than to have a nerve tapped. Nobody measures your nervous force as it runs away...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain speakers or styles (e.g., 'men of esprit' who are exhausting) can tax listeners' nerves; manage conversational exposure accordingly and value conversationalists who preserve listeners' 'nervous force.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging minds: compare thoughts with your own rather than defer to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: I had rather judge men’s minds by comparing their thoughts with my own, than judge of thoughts by knowing who utter them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form evaluations of others' ideas through independent comparison with your own standards rather than relying solely on reputation or authority of the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that small localized talents are commonly overrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Little localized powers, and little narrow streaks of specialized knowledge, are things men are very apt to be conceited about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't overvalue narrow technical accomplishments as indicators of general merit; broader humane cultivation (e.g., familiarity with books, family traditions) is preferable when other things are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social preference: other things equal, prefer a 'man of family' in society
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things being equal, in most relations of life I prefer a man of family... Four or five generations of gentlemen and gentlewomen; ... Books, family portraits, old place, claw-footed chairs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holmes lists concrete markers (family portrait gallery, old books, furniture, lineage) as signs that incline him socially toward someone raised 'in a library'; this is a prescriptive social-judgment standard in his worldview.
